title: Αἴας καὶ Ἕκτωρ
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Nestor shakes the helmet and the lot that leaps out is Ajax’s. A herald carries it round the chiefs until Ajax claims it, and he tells the army to pray, silently or aloud, to Zeus while he arms; the troops pray that he win, or at least that the two champions be equal. Ajax goes out in his bronze like Ares, with his seven-hided shield, and tells Hector he will learn that the Danaans have champions even with Achilles sulking by the ships. Hector answers that he knows war and will not strike by stealth. They exchange spear-casts, each stopped by a shield or a breastplate, and then Hector hurls a stone and Ajax a greater one, which breaks Hector’s shield and sends him down on his back until Apollo raises him. Swords are about to be drawn when the heralds Talthybius and Idaeus step between them, and Idaeus ends the fight: both are dear to Zeus, both are spearmen, and night is falling.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν, πάλλεν δὲ Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ,
ἐκ δ’ ἔθορε κλῆρος κυνέης ὃν ἄρ’ ἤθελον αὐτοὶ
Αἴαντος·
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephan, pallen de Gerēnios hippota Nestōr,
ek d’ ethore klēros kyneēs hon ar’ ēthelon autoi
Aiantos·
sentences.i: So they spoke, and the Gerenian horseman Nestor shook the helmet, and out leapt the lot that they themselves had wished for, Ajax’s;
sentences.n: Nestor shakes the helmet of the lots (it is Agamemnon’s helmet of the previous part) until one jumps out. ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν is ‘so they spoke’ and closes the army’s prayer, with ἔφαν the third-person plural imperfect of φημί; πάλλεν is an unaugmented imperfect (Attic ἔπαλλεν), ‘kept shaking’, and ἔθορε the aorist of θρῴσκω ‘leap’. Γερήνιος ἱππότα is Nestor’s standing name-epithet, ‘the Gerenian horseman’, and the meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed. κυνέης is the genitive of κυνέη ‘helmet’, governed by ἐκ; ὃν ἄρ’ ἤθελον αὐτοί is ‘which they themselves wished for’, and the unit ends on the name, Αἴαντος, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
κῆρυξ δὲ φέρων ἀν’ ὅμιλον ἁπάντῃ
δεῖξ’ ἐνδέξια πᾶσιν ἀριστήεσσιν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
kēryx de pherōn an’ homilon hapantēi
deix’ endexia pasin aristēessin Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
and a herald, bearing it through the throng all about,
showed it towards the right to all the best of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: A herald carried it through the whole throng and showed it, going round to the right, to all the best of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: The herald takes the lot round. κῆρυξ is ‘herald’, φέρων ‘bearing’, and ἀν’ ὅμιλον ἁπάντῃ ‘through the throng on every side’, with ἀνά before ὅμιλον elided. δεῖξ’ is the elided aorist of δείκνυμι ‘show’. ἐνδέξια means ‘towards the right’, the direction in which the lot goes round. ἀριστήεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ἀριστεύς, ‘best men’, and ἀριστήεσσιν Ἀχαιῶν ‘the best of the Achaeans’ is a set phrase.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ οὐ γιγνώσκοντες ἀπηνήναντο ἕκαστος.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ou gignōskontes apēnēnanto hekastos.
sentences.l: and they, not recognising it, disowned it, each one.
sentences.i: But none of them recognised it, and each disowned it.
sentences.n: The nine who threw in lots (see the previous part) all say it is not theirs. οἳ δέ ‘and they’ is the article used as a pronoun; οὐ γιγνώσκοντες is ‘not recognising’. ἀπηνήναντο is the aorist middle of ἀπαναίνομαι ‘refuse, disown’, here ‘say it is not mine’; the form is reduplicated, an old pattern for this verb. ἕκαστος ‘each one’ is singular after a plural verb.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τὸν ἵκανε φέρων ἀν’ ὅμιλον ἁπάντῃ
ὅς μιν ἐπιγράψας κυνέῃ βάλε φαίδιμος Αἴας,
ἤτοι ὑπέσχεθε χεῖρ’, ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔμβαλεν ἄγχι παραστάς,
γνῶ δὲ κλήρου σῆμα ἰδών, γήθησε δὲ θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē ton hikane pherōn an’ homilon hapantēi
hos min epigrapsas kyneēi bale phaidimos Aias,
ētoi hypeschethe cheir’, ho d’ ar’ embalen anchi parastas,
gnō de klērou sēma idōn, gēthēse de thymōi.
sentences.l:
But when now he came to the one, bearing it through the throng all about,
who, having scratched it, had cast it into the helmet, glorious Ajax,
he indeed held out his hand, and the other put it in, standing close by,
and he recognised the lot’s sign, seeing it, and rejoiced in spirit.
sentences.i: But when, carrying it through the throng, he came to the man who had scratched his mark on it and thrown it into the helmet, glorious Ajax, Ajax held out his hand, and the herald, standing close beside him, put the lot in it; and he recognised the sign of the lot when he saw it, and rejoiced in his spirit.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή … ‘but when’ runs on until the main clause at ἤτοι ὑπέσχεθε. Read τὸν … ὅς μιν ἐπιγράψας as ‘him … who had scratched it’; ἐπιγράψας is a participle of ἐπιγράφω ‘scratch on’, and the Greek says nothing more about the mark. φαίδιμος Αἴας is ‘glorious Ajax’, with the epithet always translated. ὑπέσχεθε is ‘held out’, a by-form of the aorist of ὑπέχω built on the stem σχεθ-, and ὃ δ’ ‘the other’ is the herald, who puts the lot (ἔμβαλεν) into the hand, ἄγχι παραστάς ‘standing close by’. γνῶ is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise’, and σῆμα ‘sign’ is the mark he had made.

sentences.t: τὸν μὲν πὰρ πόδ’ ἑὸν χαμάδις βάλε φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: ton men par pod’ heon chamadis bale phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: That one beside his own foot to the ground he cast, and spoke:
sentences.i: He threw it to the ground beside his foot and spoke:
sentences.n: Ajax drops the lot. τὸν μέν is the article as a pronoun, ‘that (lot)’, and μέν has no matching δέ here (φώνησέν τε follows instead). πάρ is παρά with its last vowel lost, ‘beside’; ἑόν is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative; χαμάδις is ‘to the ground’. φώνησέν τε ‘and spoke’ introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι ἤτοι κλῆρος ἐμός, χαίρω δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς
θυμῷ, ἐπεὶ δοκέω νικησέμεν Ἕκτορα δῖον.
sentences.tr:
ō philoi ētoi klēros emos, chairō de kai autos
thymōi, epei dokeō nikēsemen Hektora dion.
sentences.l:
“Friends, indeed the lot is mine, and I myself rejoice
in spirit, since I think I shall prevail over heavenly Hector.
sentences.i: “Friends, the lot is mine, and I too rejoice in my spirit, since I think I shall defeat heavenly Hector.
sentences.n: Ajax’s speech begins. ὦ φίλοι is ‘friends’; ἤτοι ‘indeed’ is a particle that stresses what follows, here the claim that the lot is his. The line is printed with ἤτοι as one word. νικησέμεν is the epic infinitive ending in -μεν for Attic νικήσειν, ‘to win, prevail’, after δοκέω ‘I think’. Ἕκτορα δῖον is ‘heavenly Hector’; δῖος is the stock epithet, always ‘heavenly’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ ὄφρ’ ἂν ἐγὼ πολεμήϊα τεύχεα δύω,
τόφρ’ ὑμεῖς εὔχεσθε Διὶ Κρονίωνι ἄνακτι
σιγῇ ἐφ’ ὑμείων ἵνα μὴ Τρῶές γε πύθωνται,
ἠὲ καὶ ἀμφαδίην, ἐπεὶ οὔ τινα δείδιμεν ἔμπης·
sentences.tr:
all’ aget’ ophr’ an egō polemēïa teuchea dyō,
tophr’ hymeis euchesthe Dii Kroniōni anakti
sigēi eph’ hymeiōn hina mē Trōes ge pythōntai,
ēe kai amphadiēn, epei ou tina deidimen empēs·
sentences.l:
But come, while I put on armour of war,
meanwhile you pray to Zeus, the son of Cronus, the lord,
in silence, by yourselves, so that the Trojans may not learn it,
or even openly, since no one do we fear, all the same;
sentences.i: But come, while I put on my armour for war, pray meanwhile to lord Zeus, the son of Cronus, in silence, by yourselves, so that the Trojans do not learn of it, or even openly, since we fear no one, all the same;
sentences.n: Ajax tells the army how to pray. ὄφρ’ ἂν ἐγὼ … δύω is ‘while I put on’ (a subjunctive with ἄν), and τόφρα answers it, ‘meanwhile’; πολεμήϊα is the adjective ‘of war’, the epic form of πολέμιος. Διὶ Κρονίωνι ἄνακτι is ‘to Zeus, the son of Cronus, the lord’. ἐφ’ ὑμείων is ἐπί with the genitive of ‘you’, ‘by yourselves, among yourselves’. ἠὲ καὶ ἀμφαδίην is ‘or even openly’. δείδιμεν is the first-person plural perfect of δείδω ‘fear’, used as a present (Attic δέδιμεν), and ἔμπης is ‘all the same’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τίς με βίῃ γε ἑκὼν ἀέκοντα δίηται
οὐδέ τι ἰδρείῃ, ἐπεὶ οὐδ’ ἐμὲ νήϊδά γ’ οὕτως
ἔλπομαι ἐν Σαλαμῖνι γενέσθαι τε τραφέμεν τε.
sentences.tr:
ou gar tis me biēi ge hekōn aekonta diētai
oude ti idreiēi, epei oud’ eme nēïda g’ houtōs
elpomai en Salamini genesthai te traphemen te.
sentences.i: for no man will drive me off by force against my will, nor by skill either, since I do not expect that I was born and reared in Salamis so ignorant as that.”
sentences.n: His reason for not fearing. οὐ γάρ τίς με … δίηται is ‘for no one … will drive me’: δίηται is a middle subjunctive of δίεμαι ‘drive away, scare’, and ἑκὼν ἀέκοντα sets one man’s will against the other’s, ‘willing’ against ‘unwilling’. βίῃ ‘by force’ and ἰδρείῃ ‘by skill’ are datives of means. νήϊδα is ‘ignorant, unknowing’, and Ajax says he does not expect to have been born and reared so, ἐν Σαλαμῖνι, on Salamis, which is his home. γενέσθαι τε τραφέμεν τε are two infinitives, and τραφέμεν is the epic -μεν form of the aorist passive τραφῆναι. His speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ εὔχοντο Διὶ Κρονίωνι ἄνακτι·
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ euchonto Dii Kroniōni anakti·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they prayed to Zeus, the son of Cronus, the lord;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they prayed to lord Zeus, the son of Cronus;
sentences.n: The prayer. ὣς ἔφαθ’ closes Ajax’s speech, with ἔφαθ’ the elided ἔφατο ‘he said’, its τ made θ before the rough breathing of οἳ. οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the Achaeans. Διὶ Κρονίωνι ἄνακτι repeats line 194 and has the same English, ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus, the lord’.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν ἰδὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν·
sentences.tr: hōde de tis eipesken idōn eis ouranon euryn·
sentences.l: And thus kept saying someone, looking to the wide heaven:
sentences.i: And thus would some man say, looking up to the wide heaven:
sentences.n: This line is word for word 7.178 in the previous part and has the same English. ὧδε is ‘thus’, and εἴπεσκεν is an iterative past of εἶπον with -σκ-, ‘would say, kept saying’, so that the prayer is what one man after another was heard to say. ἰδὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν is ‘looking to the wide heaven’.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ Ἴδηθεν μεδέων κύδιστε μέγιστε
δὸς νίκην Αἴαντι καὶ ἀγλαὸν εὖχος ἀρέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater Idēthen medeōn kydiste megiste
dos nikēn Aianti kai aglaon euchos aresthai·
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, from Ida ruling, most glorious, greatest,
give victory to Ajax, and a splendid boast to win;
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, you who rule from Ida, most glorious, greatest, give the victory to Ajax and let him win a splendid triumph;
sentences.n: The first line, Ζεῦ πάτερ Ἴδηθεν μεδέων κύδιστε μέγιστε, is a fixed address and has the English of 3.276. Ἴδηθεν ‘from Ida’ ends in the place-suffix -θεν, and μεδέων is the participle of μέδω ‘rule’; κύδιστε is ‘most glorious’. The verb is δός ‘give’, and ἀρέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἄρνυμαι, ‘to win, carry off’; εὖχος is a boast or the triumph one boasts of. ἀγλαός is ‘splendid’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ καὶ Ἕκτορά περ φιλέεις καὶ κήδεαι αὐτοῦ,
ἴσην ἀμφοτέροισι βίην καὶ κῦδος ὄπασσον.
sentences.tr:
ei de kai Hektora per phileeis kai kēdeai autou,
isēn amphoteroisi biēn kai kydos opasson.
sentences.l:
but if you also love Hector and care for him,
bestow equal might and glory on both.”
sentences.i: but if you love Hector too and care for him, bestow equal might and glory on both.”
sentences.n: The second half of the prayer asks for a draw. εἰ δὲ καὶ Ἕκτορά περ φιλέεις is ‘but if you love Hector too’, with περ stressing the name; φιλέεις is the uncontracted φιλεῖς. κήδεαι is ‘you care for’, and the genitive αὐτοῦ goes with it. ἀμφοτέροισι ‘to both’ is the dative of the persons, and ἴσην ‘equal’ agrees with βίην but goes with κῦδος in sense too, so that βίην ‘might’ and κῦδος ‘glory’ are the two things; ὄπασσον is an imperative of ὀπάζω, ‘bestow’. The prayer ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν, Αἴας δὲ κορύσσετο νώροπι χαλκῷ.
sentences.tr: hōs ar’ ephan, Aias de korysseto nōropi chalkōi.
sentences.l: So they spoke, and Ajax was arming himself in flashing bronze.
sentences.i: So they spoke, and Ajax armed himself in flashing bronze.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν ‘so they spoke’ closes the prayer. κορύσσετο is the imperfect middle of κορύσσω ‘arm’ (from κόρυς ‘helmet’), here ‘was arming himself’. νώροπι is an epithet of bronze whose meaning is not known for certain; the traditional guess is ‘flashing’, and that is the English here, as at 2.578 and in the Odyssey. χαλκῷ is the dative, ‘with bronze’, and bronze stands for the armour.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ πάντα περὶ χροῒ ἕσσατο τεύχεα,
σεύατ’ ἔπειθ’ οἷός τε πελώριος ἔρχεται Ἄρης,
ὅς τ’ εἶσιν πόλεμον δὲ μετ’ ἀνέρας οὕς τε Κρονίων
θυμοβόρου ἔριδος μένεϊ ξυνέηκε μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē panta peri chroï hessato teuchea,
seuat’ epeith’ hoios te pelōrios erchetai Arēs,
hos t’ eisin polemon de met’ aneras hous te Kroniōn
thymoborou eridos meneï xyneēke machesthai.
sentences.l:
But when he had put all the armour about his skin,
he rushed then, like huge Ares going,
who goes to war among men whom the son of Cronus
has brought together to fight by the force of heart-devouring strife.
sentences.i: And when he had put all the armour on his skin, he rushed forth like huge Ares, who goes into war among men whom the son of Cronus has set to fight with the force of heart-devouring strife.
sentences.n: A simile. ἕσσατο is the aorist middle of ἕννυμι ‘put on, clothe oneself in’, and χροΐ is the dative of χρώς ‘skin’; σεύατ’ is the aorist middle of σεύω ‘rush’. οἷός τε … Ἄρης is ‘such as Ares’, the correlative to τοῖος in the next line. πελώριος is ‘huge’. ὅς τ’ εἶσιν … is the epic τε of a general statement, ‘who goes’ whenever he goes; οὕς τε Κρονίων … ξυνέηκε is ‘those whom the son of Cronus has brought together’. θυμοβόρου is ‘heart-devouring’ (θυμός ‘heart, spirit’ + the root of βιβρώσκω ‘eat’), and ἔριδος μένεϊ ‘with the force of strife’; μένεϊ is the dative of μένος.

sentences.t:
τοῖος ἄρ’ Αἴας ὦρτο πελώριος ἕρκος Ἀχαιῶν
μειδιόων βλοσυροῖσι προσώπασι·
sentences.tr:
toios ar’ Aias ōrto pelōrios herkos Achaiōn
meidioōn blosyroisi prosōpasi·
sentences.l:
Such then rose Ajax, huge, the fence of the Achaeans,
smiling with grim faces;
sentences.i: So Ajax set forth, huge, the bulwark of the Achaeans, smiling with a grim face;
sentences.n: τοῖος ἄρ’ ‘such then’ answers οἷός τε in the simile. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, ‘rose, set out’. ἕρκος Ἀχαιῶν ‘the fence of the Achaeans’ is a stock phrase, translated ‘fence’ in the literal layer and ‘bulwark’ in the free one. μειδιόων is ‘smiling’. βλοσυροῖσι is ‘grim, fierce’ (some ancient readers took it as ‘shaggy’, so the sense is not certain), and προσώπασι is the epic plural of πρόσωπον, ‘face’.

sentences.t:
νέρθε δὲ ποσσὶν
ἤϊε μακρὰ βιβάς, κραδάων δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος.
sentences.tr:
nerthe de possin
ēïe makra bibas, kradaōn dolichoskion enchos.
sentences.l:
and beneath with his feet
he went, taking long strides, swinging his long-shadowed spear.
sentences.i: and with his feet beneath him he went on, taking long strides, swinging his long-shadowed spear.
sentences.n: νέρθε is the adverb ‘beneath’, and ποσσίν ‘with his feet’ is the old dative plural of πούς. ἤϊε is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’; μακρὰ βιβάς is ‘taking long steps’ (βιβάς is a participle of βίβημι, ‘stride’). κραδάων is ‘swinging, shaking’, from κραδάω, said of the spear. δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος ‘long-shadowed spear’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ καὶ Ἀργεῖοι μὲν ἐγήθεον εἰσορόωντες,
Τρῶας δὲ τρόμος αἰνὸς ὑπήλυθε γυῖα ἕκαστον,
Ἕκτορί τ’ αὐτῷ θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι πάτασσεν·
sentences.tr:
ton de kai Argeioi men egētheon eisoroōntes,
Trōas de tromos ainos hypēlythe guia hekaston,
Hektori t’ autōi thymos eni stēthessi patassen·
sentences.i: The Argives were glad as they looked at him, but a fearsome trembling crept over the limbs of every Trojan, and even in Hector’s own chest his heart pounded;
sentences.n: The two armies react. Ἀργεῖοι is ‘Argives’, one of the three names the poet uses for the army, and each is kept as the poet gives it. ἐγήθεον is an uncontracted imperfect, ‘were glad’, and εἰσορόωντες ‘looking at’ is the uncontracted εἰσορῶντες. Τρῶας … γυῖα ἕκαστον has the person in the accusative and the limbs in a second accusative, ‘each one in the limbs’. ὑπήλυθε is ‘crept up under’. Ἕκτορί τ’ αὐτῷ is a dative of interest, ‘for Hector himself’; στήθεσσι is the epic dative plural, and πάτασσεν is ‘pounded’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὔ πως ἔτι εἶχεν ὑποτρέσαι οὐδ’ ἀναδῦναι
ἂψ λαῶν ἐς ὅμιλον, ἐπεὶ προκαλέσσατο χάρμῃ.
sentences.tr:
all’ ou pōs eti eichen hypotresai oud’ anadynai
aps laōn es homilon, epei prokalessato charmēi.
sentences.l:
but he could no longer in any way shrink back nor draw back
again into the throng of the people, since he had challenged in the joy of battle.
sentences.i: But he could no longer shrink back or retreat into the throng of his men, since he had issued the challenge in the joy of battle.
sentences.n: Hector is committed. οὔ πως ἔτι εἶχεν is ‘he could not any longer’, with εἶχεν used as ‘was able’ and followed by two infinitives, ὑποτρέσαι ‘shrink back, flinch’ and ἀναδῦναι ‘draw back out of it’ (the aorist of ἀναδύομαι). ἂψ is ‘back again’. λαῶν is ‘of the people’, here his own men. προκαλέσσατο is the aorist middle of προκαλέω ‘call out, challenge’, and χάρμῃ is the dative of χάρμη, ‘the joy of battle’.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ ἐγγύθεν ἦλθε φέρων σάκος ἠΰτε πύργον
χάλκεον ἑπταβόειον, ὅ οἱ Τυχίος κάμε τεύχων
σκυτοτόμων ὄχ’ ἄριστος Ὕλῃ ἔνι οἰκία ναίων,
sentences.tr:
Aias d’ engythen ēlthe pherōn sakos ēÿte pyrgon
chalkeon heptaboeion, ho hoi Tychios kame teuchōn
skytotomōn och’ aristos Hylēi eni oikia naiōn,
sentences.l:
And Ajax from close by came, bearing his shield like a tower,
bronze, seven-hided, which for him Tychius toiled making,
by far the best of leather-cutters, in Hyle having his home,
sentences.i: And Ajax came up from close by, carrying a shield like a tower, of bronze, seven-hided, which Tychius had toiled to make for him, by far the best of leather-workers, who lived in his home in Hyle,
sentences.n: The shield is described, in a sentence long enough that it is cut at the comma after Ὕλῃ ἔνι οἰκία ναίων. ἠΰτε is ‘like’, and ἐγγύθεν ‘from close by’ ends in the place-suffix -θεν. ἑπταβόειον is ‘seven-hided’, from ἑπτά ‘seven’ and βόειος ‘of an ox’, so seven ox-hides, with bronze for the face (χάλκεον). ὅ οἱ … κάμε τεύχων is ‘which for him he toiled making’, with the unaugmented aorist κάμε. Τυχίος is a name; σκυτοτόμων ὄχ’ ἄριστος is ‘by far the best of leather-cutters’, that is, workers in hide. Ὕλῃ is a place name in the dative, ‘in Hyle’, and οἰκία ναίων ‘living in his home’.

sentences.t:
ὅς οἱ ἐποίησεν σάκος αἰόλον ἑπταβόειον
ταύρων ζατρεφέων, ἐπὶ δ’ ὄγδοον ἤλασε χαλκόν.
sentences.tr:
hos hoi epoiēsen sakos aiolon heptaboeion
taurōn zatrepheōn, epi d’ ogdoon ēlase chalkon.
sentences.l:
who made him the glancing shield, seven-hided,
of sleek bulls, and on top as the eighth he drove bronze.
sentences.i: He made him the glancing shield, seven-hided, from well-fed bulls, and hammered on top of it an eighth layer, of bronze.
sentences.n: This continues the description. ὅς οἱ ἐποίησεν is ‘who made for him’. αἰόλον is ‘glancing, quick-moving’, the same word that sits inside κορυθαίολος. ζατρεφέων is ‘well-fed’ in the free English and ‘sleek’ in the literal, as for ζατρεφέας in the Odyssey (4.451); ζα- is an intensive prefix on τρέφω ‘nourish’, said here of bulls. ἐπὶ δ’ ὄγδοον ἤλασε χαλκόν is ‘and on top he drove an eighth, of bronze’: ἤλασε, from ἐλαύνω, has the sense ‘beat out’ for metal, so the eighth layer is a plate of bronze over seven hides.

sentences.t:
τὸ πρόσθε στέρνοιο φέρων Τελαμώνιος Αἴας
στῆ ῥα μάλ’ Ἕκτορος ἐγγύς, ἀπειλήσας δὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
to prosthe sternoio pherōn Telamōnios Aias
stē rha mal’ Hektoros engys, apeilēsas de prosēuda·
sentences.l:
This before his breast bearing, Telamonian Ajax
stood very near Hector, and having threatened, addressed him:
sentences.i: Holding this before his chest, Telamonian Ajax stood very near Hector and addressed him with threats:
sentences.n: τό is ‘this’, the shield. Τελαμώνιος Αἴας is ‘Telamonian Ajax’, the adjective telling him from the other Ajax. στέρνοιο is ‘of the breast’, a genitive of place with πρόσθε ‘in front of’. στῆ ῥα is ‘stood then’; ἐγγύς governs Ἕκτορος. ἀπειλήσας is ‘having threatened’, and προσηύδα ‘addressed’, an imperfect of προσαυδάω. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ νῦν μὲν δὴ σάφα εἴσεαι οἰόθεν οἶος
οἷοι καὶ Δαναοῖσιν ἀριστῆες μετέασι
καὶ μετ’ Ἀχιλλῆα ῥηξήνορα θυμολέοντα.
sentences.tr:
Hektor nyn men dē sapha eiseai oiothen oios
hoioi kai Danaoisin aristēes meteasi
kai met’ Achillēa rhēxēnora thymoleonta.
sentences.l:
“Hector, now indeed you will know clearly, singly, alone,
what sort of best men there are among the Danaans too,
even after Achilles, man-breaking, lion-hearted.
sentences.i: “Hector, now you will learn clearly, all alone, what kind of best men there are among the Danaans too, even after Achilles, the man-breaker, the lion-hearted.
sentences.n: Ajax’s speech. σάφα εἴσεαι ‘you will know clearly’ has the epic future εἴσεαι of οἶδα. οἰόθεν οἶος is ‘singly, alone’ (as at 7.39), here of a man who stands alone against another. οἷοι … ἀριστῆες ‘what sort of best men’ is a clause object of ‘know’, and Δαναοῖσιν ‘among the Danaans’ is another of the army’s three names. μετ’ Ἀχιλλῆα is ‘after Achilles’, that is, next to him in rank, and the name has a single λ for the metre. ῥηξήνορα ‘man-breaking’ is from ῥήγνυμι ‘break’ and ἀνήρ, and whether it means a breaker of ranks or a killer of men is not known. θυμολέοντα is ‘lion-hearted’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἐν νήεσσι κορωνίσι ποντοπόροισι
κεῖτ’ ἀπομηνίσας Ἀγαμέμνονι ποιμένι λαῶν·
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men en nēessi korōnisi pontoporoisi
keit’ apomēnisas Agamemnoni poimeni laōn·
sentences.l:
But he among the curved, sea-crossing ships
lay, withdrawn in wrath at Agamemnon, shepherd of the people;
sentences.i: But he lay among the curved, sea-crossing ships, withdrawn in wrath at Agamemnon, shepherd of the people;
sentences.n: These two lines are word for word 2.771–772, where the sentence went on to name Agamemnon as the son of Atreus; here it stops at λαῶν, and the English is the published English. ὃ μέν ‘he’ is Achilles. κορωνίσι ποντοπόροισι is ‘curved, sea-crossing’. κεῖτ’ is the imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lie’, and ἀπομηνίσας ‘withdrawn in wrath’ is a participle of μηνίω with ἀπο-, whose force is not certain. Ἀγαμέμνονι ποιμένι λαῶν is ‘Agamemnon, shepherd of the people’.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ εἰμὲν τοῖοι οἳ ἂν σέθεν ἀντιάσαιμεν
καὶ πολέες·
sentences.tr:
hēmeis d’ eimen toioi hoi an sethen antiasaimen
kai polees·
sentences.l:
But we are such as might meet you,
and many;
sentences.i: But there are men among us who could face you, and many of them;
sentences.n: εἰμέν is the epic form of ἐσμέν ‘we are’. τοῖοι οἳ ἂν σέθεν ἀντιάσαιμεν is ‘such that we could meet you’: τοῖοι is ‘such’, a plural in -οι, the optative ἀντιάσαιμεν with ἄν expresses what could be, and σέθεν is an epic genitive of σύ. καὶ πολέες ‘and many’ is πολλοί with its epic ending.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄρχε μάχης ἠδὲ πτολέμοιο.
sentences.tr: all’ arche machēs ēde ptolemoio.
sentences.l: but begin the battle and the war.”
sentences.i: But begin the battle and the war.”
sentences.n: ἄρχε is the imperative of ἄρχω, here with the genitive, ‘begin’. μάχης ἠδὲ πτολέμοιο is ‘battle and war’, with πτολέμοιο the epic variant of πολέμοιο. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe megas korythaiolos Hektōr·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed great Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Then great Hector of the glancing helmet spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the formula of a reply, ‘and him in turn addressed’. κορυθαίολος is built from κόρυς ‘helmet’ and αἰόλος ‘glancing, quick-moving’, so it is ‘of the glancing helmet’, always rendered so; μέγας is ‘great’.

sentences.t:
Αἶαν διογενὲς Τελαμώνιε κοίρανε λαῶν
μή τί μευ ἠΰτε παιδὸς ἀφαυροῦ πειρήτιζε
ἠὲ γυναικός, ἣ οὐκ οἶδεν πολεμήϊα ἔργα.
sentences.tr:
Aian diogenes Telamōnie koirane laōn
mē ti meu ēÿte paidos aphaurou peirētize
ēe gynaikos, hē ouk oiden polemēïa erga.
sentences.l:
“Ajax, Zeus-sprung, Telamonian, ruler of the people,
not at all like a weak boy make trial of me,
or of a woman, who knows not the works of war.
sentences.i: “Zeus-born Ajax, Telamonian, ruler of the people, do not make trial of me as though I were a weak boy, or a woman who knows nothing of the works of war.
sentences.n: Hector answers. Αἶαν is the vocative of Αἴας; διογενές ‘Zeus-sprung’ and κοίρανε λαῶν ‘ruler of the people’ pile up the titles. μή τί μευ … πειρήτιζε is a prohibition, ‘do not at all make trial of me’, with μευ the epic genitive of ἐγώ. ἠΰτε is ‘like’, παιδὸς ἀφαυροῦ ‘a weak boy’, and ἠὲ γυναικός ‘or a woman’. ἣ οὐκ οἶδεν is ‘who does not know’, and πολεμήϊα ἔργα is ‘the works of war’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν εὖ οἶδα μάχας τ’ ἀνδροκτασίας τε·
sentences.tr: autar egōn eu oida machas t’ androktasias te·
sentences.l: but I well know battles and man-slayings;
sentences.i: But I know well battles and man-slayings;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν εὖ οἶδα begins a list in which every clause is ‘I know’. ἐγών is an epic form of ἐγώ. μάχας ‘battles’ and ἀνδροκτασίας ‘man-slayings’ (from ἀνήρ and κτείνω) are the two things he knows.

sentences.t:
οἶδ’ ἐπὶ δεξιά, οἶδ’ ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ νωμῆσαι βῶν
ἀζαλέην, τό μοι ἔστι ταλαύρινον πολεμίζειν·
sentences.tr:
oid’ epi dexia, oid’ ep’ aristera nōmēsai bōn
azaleēn, to moi esti talaurinon polemizein·
sentences.l:
I know to the right, I know to the left to wield
the dry ox-hide, which for me is shield-enduring, to fight;
sentences.i: I know how to wield the dry ox-hide to the right and to the left, and that is how I am able to fight on, steadfast in my shield;
sentences.n: βῶν is ‘ox’ for its hide, that is, the shield made of it. ἀζαλέην is ‘dry’. νωμῆσαι is an aorist infinitive of νωμάω ‘wield’. ταλαύρινον is a rare word whose meaning is uncertain: it seems to join τλάω ‘endure’ and ῥινός ‘hide’, the hide being the shield, so the literal English is ‘shield-enduring’ and the free ‘steadfast in my shield’, which is a guess. τό μοι ἔστι is ‘which for me is’, and πολεμίζειν the infinitive ‘to fight’.

sentences.t: οἶδα δ’ ἐπαΐξαι μόθον ἵππων ὠκειάων·
sentences.tr: oida d’ epaïxai mothon hippōn ōkeiaōn·
sentences.l: and I know to rush upon the press of swift horses;
sentences.i: I know how to charge into the press of swift horses;
sentences.n: ἐπαΐξαι is the aorist infinitive of ἐπαΐσσω ‘rush at’. μόθον is ‘press’, the crush of battle; here it is the crush of the chariot-horses, ἵππων ὠκειάων, with the epic genitive plural in -άων.

sentences.t: οἶδα δ’ ἐνὶ σταδίῃ δηΐῳ μέλπεσθαι Ἄρηϊ.
sentences.tr: oida d’ eni stadiēi dēïōi melpesthai Arēï.
sentences.l: and I know in the standing fight to dance for hostile Ares.
sentences.i: And I know how to dance the dance of hostile war in the fight where men stand their ground.
sentences.n: μέλπεσθαι is ‘to dance (and sing)’, here a metaphor for fighting; Ἄρηϊ is the dative of Ἄρης, who is the god and also war itself, so the English keeps ‘Ares’ in the literal layer and ‘war’ in the free one. σταδίῃ is ‘standing’, understood as a fight in which men do not give way, and δηΐῳ is ‘hostile’. The unit ends at the full stop.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ γάρ σ’ ἐθέλω βαλέειν τοιοῦτον ἐόντα
λάθρῃ ὀπιπεύσας, ἀλλ’ ἀμφαδόν, αἴ κε τύχωμι.
sentences.tr:
all’ ou gar s’ ethelō baleein toiouton eonta
lathrēi opipeusas, all’ amphadon, ai ke tychōmi.
sentences.l:
But I do not wish to strike you, being such a man,
by stealth, spying on you, but openly, if I can hit.”
sentences.i: But I do not want to strike a man like you by stealth, after watching for my chance, but openly, if I can hit you.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐ γάρ is ‘but no, for’. βαλέειν is the epic infinitive of βάλλω ‘strike with a missile’, and τοιοῦτον ἐόντα ‘being such a man’. λάθρῃ is ‘by stealth’; ὀπιπεύσας is ‘having spied’. ἀμφαδόν is ‘openly’, like ἀμφαδίην in line 196. αἴ κε τύχωμι is ‘if I should hit’, with the rare first-person subjunctive ending -μι. His speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἀμπεπαλὼν προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος,
καὶ βάλεν Αἴαντος δεινὸν σάκος ἑπταβόειον
ἀκρότατον κατὰ χαλκόν, ὃς ὄγδοος ἦεν ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr:
ē rha, kai ampepalōn proïei dolichoskion enchos,
kai balen Aiantos deinon sakos heptaboeion
akrotaton kata chalkon, hos ogdoos ēen ep’ autōi.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and having brandished it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear,
and hit the dread seven-hided shield of Ajax
upon the topmost bronze, which was the eighth upon it.
sentences.i: So he said, and brandishing it he sent forth his long-shadowed spear, and hit Ajax’s dread seven-hided shield on the topmost bronze, which was the eighth layer on it.
sentences.n: The exchange of blows begins. The first line has the English of 3.355 (ἦ ῥα, καί, ‘he spoke, and’; ἀμπεπαλών ‘having brandished’; προΐει ‘sent forth’). δεινόν is ‘dread’, ἑπταβόειον ‘seven-hided’, as in line 220. ἀκρότατον κατὰ χαλκόν is ‘on the topmost bronze’, the outer plate. ὃς ὄγδοος ἦεν ἐπ’ αὐτῷ is ‘which was the eighth upon it’ (ἦεν the epic ἦν), and this is the plate of line 223.

sentences.t:
ἓξ δὲ διὰ πτύχας ἦλθε δαΐζων χαλκὸς ἀτειρής,
ἐν τῇ δ’ ἑβδομάτῃ ῥινῷ σχέτο·
sentences.tr:
hex de dia ptychas ēlthe daïzōn chalkos ateirēs,
en tēi d’ hebdomatēi rhinōi scheto·
sentences.l:
And through six folds went, rending them, the unwearied bronze,
but in the seventh hide it was stopped;
sentences.i: The unwearied bronze went through six folds, rending them, and was stopped in the seventh hide;
sentences.n: The spear is the bronze here. ἓξ δὲ διὰ πτύχας is ‘and through six folds’, with διά ‘through’ governing πτύχας ‘folds’, the layers of hide. δαΐζων is ‘rending’. ἀτειρής ‘unwearied’ is a stock epithet of bronze, from ἀ- and τείρω ‘wear down’. ἑβδομάτῃ ῥινῷ is ‘the seventh hide’, and σχέτο is the aorist middle of ἔχω, ‘was stopped’. The unit ends at the ano teleia, in the middle of line 248.

sentences.t:
δεύτερος αὖτε
Αἴας διογενὴς προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος,
καὶ βάλε Πριαμίδαο κατ’ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην.
sentences.tr:
deuteros aute
Aias diogenēs proïei dolichoskion enchos,
kai bale Priamidao kat’ aspida pantos’ eïsēn.
sentences.i: Then Zeus-born Ajax, in his turn, sent forth his long-shadowed spear, and hit the son of Priam on his shield, equal on every side;
sentences.n: δεύτερος αὖτε is ‘second, in turn’. διογενής is ‘Zeus-sprung’. The last line is nearly 3.356: Πριαμίδαο is ‘the son of Priam’ (Hector), and the shield is πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην, ‘equal on every side’, where ἐΐσην is an old longer form of ἴσην and means a shield that is round and balanced.

sentences.t:
διὰ μὲν ἀσπίδος ἦλθε φαεινῆς ὄβριμον ἔγχος,
καὶ διὰ θώρηκος πολυδαιδάλου ἠρήρειστο·
sentences.tr:
dia men aspidos ēlthe phaeinēs obrimon enchos,
kai dia thōrēkos polydaidalou ērēreisto·
sentences.l:
Through the shining shield went the mighty spear,
and through the much-wrought breastplate it was driven;
sentences.i: The mighty spear went through the shining shield, and was driven through the richly wrought breastplate as well;
sentences.n: These two lines are word for word 3.357–358, with the same English. Line 251 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of διά, short by nature, has to be read long to fill the first foot. ὄβριμον is ‘mighty’, φαεινῆς ‘shining’, πολυδαιδάλου ‘much-wrought, richly wrought’, and ἠρήρειστο is the pluperfect passive of ἐρείδω ‘press, drive’.

sentences.t:
ἀντικρὺ δὲ παραὶ λαπάρην διάμησε χιτῶνα
ἔγχος·
sentences.tr:
antikry de parai laparēn diamēse chitōna
enchos·
sentences.l:
and straight on, along the flank, it cut through the tunic,
the spear;
sentences.i: and straight on, along his flank, the spear cut through the tunic;
sentences.n: The unit is word for word 3.359 with the first word of 3.360, and has the same English. ἀντικρύ is ‘straight on’, παραὶ λαπάρην ‘along the flank’, and διάμησε ‘cut through’. The subject, ἔγχος, is held back to the start of the next line, and it is Ajax’s spear.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐκλίνθη καὶ ἀλεύατο κῆρα μέλαιναν.
sentences.tr: ho d’ eklinthē kai aleuato kēra melainan.
sentences.l: but he leaned away and avoided the black death-fate.
sentences.i: but he swerved aside and avoided the black spirit of death.
sentences.n: The half-line is word for word 3.360, with the same English. ὃ δ’ ‘but he’ is Hector. ἐκλίνθη is ‘leaned away’; ἀλεύατο is the aorist middle of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’; κῆρα μέλαιναν is ‘the black death-fate’, κήρ meaning a spirit of death and not the word for ‘heart’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἐκσπασσαμένω δολίχ’ ἔγχεα χερσὶν ἅμ’ ἄμφω
σύν ῥ’ ἔπεσον λείουσιν ἐοικότες ὠμοφάγοισιν
ἢ συσὶ κάπροισιν, τῶν τε σθένος οὐκ ἀλαπαδνόν.
sentences.tr:
tō d’ ekspassamenō dolich’ enchea chersin ham’ amphō
syn rh’ epeson leiousin eoikotes ōmophagoisin
ē sysi kaproisin, tōn te sthenos ouk alapadnon.
sentences.l:
And the two, having drawn out their long spears with their hands, both together,
fell upon each other, like raw-eating lions
or wild boars, whose strength is not feeble.
sentences.i: The two of them pulled out their long spears with their hands, both at once, and fell on each other like lions that eat raw flesh, or wild boars, whose strength is not feeble.
sentences.n: τώ is the dual of the article, ‘the two’, with ἐκσπασσαμένω a dual participle, ‘having drawn out’. δολίχ’ ἔγχεα is ‘long spears’, and ἅμ’ ἄμφω ‘both together’. σὺν … ἔπεσον is tmesis, the preverb standing apart: ‘fell together, clashed’. The simile has the English published at 5.782–783: λείουσιν … ὠμοφάγοισιν ‘raw-eating lions’ and ἢ συσὶ κάπροισιν, τῶν τε σθένος οὐκ ἀλαπαδνόν ‘or wild boars, whose strength is not feeble’.

sentences.t:
Πριαμίδης μὲν ἔπειτα μέσον σάκος οὔτασε δουρί,
οὐδ’ ἔρρηξεν χαλκός, ἀνεγνάμφθη δέ οἱ αἰχμή.
sentences.tr:
Priamidēs men epeita meson sakos outase douri,
oud’ errēxen chalkos, anegnamphthē de hoi aichmē.
sentences.l:
Priam’s-son then in the middle of the shield struck with his spear,
and the bronze did not break it, and its point was bent back.
sentences.i: Then the son of Priam struck the middle of the shield with his spear, but the bronze did not break it, and its point was bent back.
sentences.n: Πριαμίδης is ‘Priam’s-son’, Hector, as Ἀτρεΐδης is ‘Atreus’-son’. μέσον σάκος is ‘the middle of the shield’, and οὔτασε ‘struck’ is an aorist of οὐτάζω, said of a blow with a thrust. οὐδ’ ἔρρηξεν χαλκός ‘the bronze did not break it’ and ἀνεγνάμφθη δέ οἱ αἰχμή ‘and its point was bent back’ have the English of 3.348; ἀνεγνάμφθη is the aorist passive of ἀναγνάμπτω, and αἰχμή ‘point’ is the spearhead.

sentences.t: Αἴας δ’ ἀσπίδα νύξεν ἐπάλμενος·
sentences.tr: Aias d’ aspida nyxen epalmenos·
sentences.l: And Ajax stabbed the shield, leaping upon him;
sentences.i: Then Ajax sprang forward and stabbed the shield;
sentences.n: νύξεν is the aorist of νύσσω ‘prick, stab’, without augment. ἐπάλμενος is the aorist participle of ἐφάλλομαι ‘spring upon’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ διαπρὸ
ἤλυθεν ἐγχείη, στυφέλιξε δέ μιν μεμαῶτα,
τμήδην δ’ αὐχέν’ ἐπῆλθε, μέλαν δ’ ἀνεκήκιεν αἷμα,
sentences.tr:
hē de diapro
ēlythen encheiē, styphelixe de min memaōta,
tmēdēn d’ auchen’ epēlthe, melan d’ anekēkien haima,
sentences.l:
and right through it
went the spear, and thrust him roughly, eager as he was,
cutting it passed over his neck, and dark blood welled up,
sentences.i: and the spear went right through it and shoved him, eager as he was, and cut along his neck, and dark blood welled up,
sentences.n: ἣ δὲ διαπρὸ ἤλυθεν ἐγχείη is ‘and right through it went the spear’: ἣ is the article used as a pronoun, ἐγχείη the spear, and διαπρό ‘right through’; ἤλυθεν is an aorist of ἔρχομαι. The sentence runs on for six lines, so the unit is cut at the comma after αἷμα. στυφέλιξε is ‘thrust roughly, shoved’, and μεμαῶτα ‘eager’ is the perfect participle of μέμονα. τμήδην is an adverb from τέμνω ‘cut’, ‘with a cutting’; it says the spear cut the neck, and the Greek does not say how deeply. μέλαν … αἷμα is ‘dark blood’, ἀνεκήκιεν ‘welled up’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς ἀπέληγε μάχης κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ,
ἀλλ’ ἀναχασσάμενος λίθον εἵλετο χειρὶ παχείῃ
κείμενον ἐν πεδίῳ μέλανα τρηχύν τε μέγαν τε·
sentences.tr:
all’ oud’ hōs apelēge machēs korythaiolos Hektōr,
all’ anachassamenos lithon heileto cheiri pacheiēi
keimenon en pediōi melana trēchyn te megan te·
sentences.i: But even so Hector of the glancing helmet did not leave off the fight; he drew back and took in his stout hand a stone that lay on the plain, black and rough and great;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς is ‘but not even so’. ἀπέληγε is ‘left off, ceased from’, with μάχης ‘from the fight’ in the genitive. κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ is ‘Hector of the glancing helmet’. ἀναχασσάμενος is ‘drawing back’, an aorist middle participle. χειρὶ παχείῃ is ‘with a stout hand’. κείμενον ἐν πεδίῳ is ‘lying in the plain’, and μέλανα τρηχύν τε μέγαν τε are the stone’s three qualities, ‘black, rough, great’.

sentences.t:
τῷ βάλεν Αἴαντος δεινὸν σάκος ἑπταβόειον
μέσσον ἐπομφάλιον·
sentences.tr:
tōi balen Aiantos deinon sakos heptaboeion
messon epomphalion·
sentences.l:
With it he hit the dread seven-hided shield of Ajax
in the middle, on the boss;
sentences.i: With it he hit Ajax’s dread seven-hided shield right in the middle, on the boss;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘with it’, the stone. The shield is the same as in line 245, and the English is the same. ἐπομφάλιον is ‘on the boss’, from ἐπί and ὀμφαλός, the knob at the centre, whose name is also ‘navel’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 267.

sentences.t: περιήχησεν δ’ ἄρα χαλκός.
sentences.tr: periēchēsen d’ ara chalkos.
sentences.l: and the bronze rang all round.
sentences.i: and the bronze rang all around.
sentences.n: περιήχησεν is ‘rang round’, with περι- ‘all round’. The bronze is the shield-plate, and the Greek gives the sound with no comment on its effect.

sentences.t:
δεύτερος αὖτ’ Αἴας πολὺ μείζονα λᾶαν ἀείρας
ἧκ’ ἐπιδινήσας, ἐπέρεισε δὲ ἶν’ ἀπέλεθρον,
εἴσω δ’ ἀσπίδ’ ἔαξε βαλὼν μυλοειδέϊ πέτρῳ,
βλάψε δέ οἱ φίλα γούναθ’·
sentences.tr:
deuteros aut’ Aias poly meizona laan aeiras
hēk’ epidinēsas, epereise de in’ apelethron,
eisō d’ aspid’ eaxe balōn myloeideï petrōi,
blapse de hoi phila gounath’·
sentences.l:
Second, in turn, Ajax a much greater stone lifting
hurled it, having swung it round, and pressed upon it strength immeasurable,
and inward he broke the shield, striking with the millstone-like rock,
and hurt his dear knees;
sentences.i: Then Ajax in his turn lifted a much greater stone and, swinging it round, hurled it, and put immeasurable strength behind it, and broke the shield inward, striking it with the rock like a millstone, and hurt Hector’s knees;
sentences.n: δεύτερος αὖτ’ is ‘second, in turn’. The second line is word for word Odyssey 9.538 and has its English, except that ἶν’ ἀπέλεθρον takes the English of 5.245, ‘strength immeasurable’, where the Odyssey says ‘measureless’: ἧκ’ is ‘hurled’, ἐπιδινήσας ‘having swung it round’, and ἐπέρεισε ‘pressed upon it’ (ἀπέλεθρος may come from πέλεθρον, a measure of length, but this is not certain). εἴσω is ‘inward’, and ἔαξε is the aorist of ἄγνυμι ‘break’. μυλοειδέϊ πέτρῳ is ‘a rock like a millstone’. βλάψε is ‘hurt, disabled’, and φίλα here is ‘his own’, the possessive sense of φίλος, so the knees are Hector’s.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὕπτιος ἐξετανύσθη
ἀσπίδι ἐγχριμφθείς·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ hyptios exetanysthē
aspidi enchrimphtheis·
sentences.l:
and he was stretched out on his back,
pressed against his shield;
sentences.i: and he was stretched out on his back, driven hard against his shield;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Hector. ὕπτιος is ‘on his back’, ἐξετανύσθη ‘was stretched out’ (the aorist passive of ἐκτανύω). ἐγχριμφθείς is a participle of ἐγχρίμπτω ‘press close, drive against’, so Hector falls with his own shield pushed against him. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 272.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αἶψ’ ὤρθωσεν Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.tr: ton d’ aips’ ōrthōsen Apollōn.
sentences.l: and him quickly set upright Apollo.
sentences.i: but Apollo quickly set him upright.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ‘but him’ is Hector. ὤρθωσεν is the aorist of ὀρθόω ‘set upright’, and αἶψ’ ‘quickly’. Apollo’s help comes in one short clause and the poet does not say how he does it.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κε δὴ ξιφέεσσ’ αὐτοσχεδὸν οὐτάζοντο,
εἰ μὴ κήρυκες Διὸς ἄγγελοι ἠδὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν
ἦλθον, ὃ μὲν Τρώων, ὃ δ’ Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων,
Ταλθύβιός τε καὶ Ἰδαῖος πεπνυμένω ἄμφω·
sentences.tr:
kai ny ke dē xipheess’ autoschedon outazonto,
ei mē kērykes Dios angeloi ēde kai andrōn
ēlthon, ho men Trōōn, ho d’ Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn,
Talthybios te kai Idaios pepnymenō amphō·
sentences.i: And now they would have been striking each other with swords at close quarters, had the heralds not come, the messengers of Zeus and of men as well, one for the Trojans and one for the bronze-shirted Achaeans, Talthybius and Idaeus, both prudent men;
sentences.n: καί νύ κε δή … οὐτάζοντο is a past ‘would have been’ in a condition that never came true: κε with the imperfect, and εἰ μή ‘if … not’ names what stopped it. αὐτοσχεδόν is ‘at close quarters’, and ξιφέεσσ’ the epic dative plural of ξίφος ‘sword’. κήρυκες Διὸς ἄγγελοι ἠδὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν is ‘heralds, messengers of Zeus and also of men’. ὃ μὲν Τρώων, ὃ δ’ Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων is ‘the one of the Trojans, the other of the bronze-shirted Achaeans’. πεπνυμένω ἄμφω is ‘the two prudent’, in the dual.

sentences.t:
μέσσῳ δ’ ἀμφοτέρων σκῆπτρα σχέθον, εἶπέ τε μῦθον
κῆρυξ Ἰδαῖος πεπνυμένα μήδεα εἰδώς·
sentences.tr:
messōi d’ amphoterōn skēptra schethon, eipe te mython
kēryx Idaios pepnymena mēdea eidōs·
sentences.l:
and between the two they held their sceptres, and spoke a word,
the herald Idaeus, prudent counsels knowing;
sentences.i: and held their sceptres between the two, and the herald Idaeus, a man versed in prudent counsels, spoke:
sentences.n: μέσσῳ ἀμφοτέρων is ‘in the middle of both’. σκῆπτρα σχέθον is ‘held (their) sceptres’, σχέθον an aorist of ἔχω, the sceptre being the herald’s sign of office. εἶπέ τε μῦθον … κῆρυξ Ἰδαῖος is ‘and spoke a word, the herald Idaeus’, with the subject held back to the second line. πεπνυμένα μήδεα εἰδώς, ‘knowing prudent counsels’, is a standing phrase, which the free English gives as ‘a man versed in prudent counsels’.

sentences.t: μηκέτι παῖδε φίλω πολεμίζετε μηδὲ μάχεσθον·
sentences.tr: mēketi paide philō polemizete mēde machesthon·
sentences.l: “No longer, dear sons, make war, nor fight;
sentences.i: “Dear sons, make war no longer, and do not fight;
sentences.n: Idaeus speaks to the two. μηκέτι … πολεμίζετε is a prohibition of something already going on, ‘stop making war’; the address is a dual, παῖδε φίλω ‘dear sons’, and the verbs are plural (πολεμίζετε) and then dual (μάχεσθον), a mixture the poet allows. The herald’s ‘sons’ is a term of affection, not of kinship.

sentences.t:
ἀμφοτέρω γὰρ σφῶϊ φιλεῖ νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς,
ἄμφω δ’ αἰχμητά·
sentences.tr:
amphoterō gar sphōï philei nephelēgereta Zeus,
amphō d’ aichmēta·
sentences.l:
for both of you loves cloud-gatherer Zeus,
and both spearmen;
sentences.i: for Zeus who gathers the clouds loves you both, and you are both spearmen;
sentences.n: ἀμφοτέρω γὰρ σφῶϊ is ‘for both of you’, using the dual pronoun σφῶϊ. φιλεῖ is ‘loves’, and νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς is ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’, translated every time. ἄμφω δ’ αἰχμητά is ‘and both spearmen’, αἰχμητά being the dual of αἰχμητής. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 281.

sentences.t: τό γε δὴ καὶ ἴδμεν ἅπαντες.
sentences.tr: to ge dē kai idmen hapantes.
sentences.l: this indeed we also know, all of us.
sentences.i: and that we all know.
sentences.n: τό γε δή is ‘that indeed’, pointing back at what has just been said. ἴδμεν is the epic form of ἴσμεν ‘we know’, and καί ‘also’ adds that everyone knows it.

sentences.t: νὺξ δ’ ἤδη τελέθει·
sentences.tr: nyx d’ ēdē telethei·
sentences.l: and night is already here;
sentences.i: night is already here;
sentences.n: τελέθει is a present of τελέθω, ‘be, come to be’; with νύξ, ‘night’, it says that night has arrived. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: ἀγαθὸν καὶ νυκτὶ πιθέσθαι.
sentences.tr: agathon kai nykti pithesthai.
sentences.l: it is good also to obey night.”
sentences.i: it is good to yield to night as well.”
sentences.n: ἀγαθόν ‘good’ has ἐστί understood. πιθέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of the middle of πείθω, ‘to obey, give way to’; the dative νυκτί is the one obeyed, and καί means ‘also’. Idaeus’ speech ends here.
